entries.title: AI chip smugglers exploit trade control loophole to bring banned HBM from South Korea into China — expensive memory chips packaged with cheap, unsanctioned processors to become legal exports | Tom's Hardware
entries.paragraph_1: A memory smuggler has detailed how he gets export-controlled HBM chips from South Korea into China using a loophole. According to The Information , the smuggler owns a chip design firm that build cheap, low-performing processors that fall under the U.S. and South Korea’s export controls. They are then paired with expensive HBM from Samsung and SK hynix, that, on their own, are banned for export to China. But because export control rules only look at the performance of the server processor and not at the other components attached to it, this allows the HBM chips attached inside them to slip under the radar and make their way into China.
entries.paragraph_2: It’s not a risk-free operation, though. Once the mediocre processors with high-end memory chips land in Hong Kong and are smuggled across the border into Shenzhen in the luggage of commuters that cross between the two regions daily, they end up in workshops where technicians heat up the boards to soften the solder, gingerly lift the crucial memory chips, and discard the rest of the components. Despite having a high failure rate, the high price of HBM chips makes the procedure quite lucrative.

entries.paragraph_2: The driver is structural, not cyclical. entries.paragraph_2: The Pyongyang Declaration will be printed in the government gazette within a few days, while the CMA is supposed to be printed after sharing the text with North Korea. From the moment the two inter-Korean summit agreements are printed in the government gazette, they will become legally binding.

entries.title: Binance Theft Wasn't Us: North Korea
entries.paragraph_1: North Korea on Tuesday denied involvement in the cryptocurrency heist at Binance, dismissing as a provocation the US announcement that North Korean hackers were behind the theft. Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange, said Friday that hackers stole more than $6 billion in what appears to be the largest cryptocurrency theft on record, per the AP . The FBI later said the crime was orchestrated by North Korean hackers, attributing the attack to TraderTraitor, the hacking group that was behind a $1.5 billion hack of the Bybit exchange last year.
entries.paragraph_2: Kim Yo Jong, the influential sister of North Korean ruler Kim Jong Un, called the FBI announcement "a trite provocation" and "an absurd rhetoric" on Tuesday. "This is not the first time that the US has attempted to spread misunderstanding of the DPRK in the international community, blindly linking the DPRK with the 'cyber crime' incidents whenever they occur on an international scale," she said in a statement, using the abbreviation of North Korea's official name, the Democratic People's Republic of Korea. She added that the accusation "confirmed Washington's hostile attitude."

entries.paragraph_1: Korean conglomerates are rapidly shifting global business operations from China to the US. China, meanwhile, fell to second place as the number of overseas affiliates there fell from 700 to 529, accounting for 10.7% of the total.

North Korea Maintains Nuclear-Armed Status North Korea continues to reject disarmament and has enshrined its status as a nuclear-armed state in law. Pyongyang has ruled out giving up its weapons, a stance that has outlasted successive rounds of diplomacy and pressure campaigns. The Northâs position rests on a security calculation that outside analysts have long described: the regime views its arsenal as the ultimate guarantee against external pressure, and it has shown little willingness to trade that guarantee for economic relief alone [2] . Academic assessments of nuclear proliferation have noted that the most consequential step in the process is the acquisition of fissile material, and that once a state crosses that threshold, reversing course becomes substantially harder [2] . The North is backed by Russia and China, whose diplomatic cover has blunted international enforcement. Moscow and Beijing have worked to soften successive rounds of sanctions, according to published analyses of the Security Council process [3] . That support has given Pyongyang room to weather restrictions that would otherwise have imposed higher costs. North Korea also denounced a Saturday joint statement by a group of nations monitoring sanctions implementation. Trump Overtures and APEC Summit Speculation Speculation is mounting over a possible meeting between the U.S. and North Korea. The APEC summit would provide a venue for a leaders-level encounter without the formal preparation that a dedicated bilateral summit would require. The proposal marked a shift in emphasis from the position the three allies restated in Atlanta. Critics have said such an approach risks tacitly accepting North Korea as a nuclear-armed state and allowing Pyongyang to obtain sanctions relief without giving up its arsenal. The debate turns on whether a freeze would lock in the Northâs capabilities or serve as a first step toward broader limits. Analysts say China may also be moving toward tacit acceptance. They point to the omission of North Korean denuclearization from statements issued after North Korean leader Kim Jong-Un and Chinese President Xi Jinping met in June. The omission, analysts argue, could signal that Beijing is prepared to treat the Northâs arsenal as a settled fact rather than a negotiating objective. The competing positions leave the three allies with a stated goal of complete denuclearization and an array of tactical options that range from pressure to conditional engagement. entries.title: US, South Korea and Japan Renew Commitment to North Korea’s Denuclearization
entries.paragraph_1: The United States, South Korea and Japan have renewed their commitment to the “complete denuclearization” of North Korea as Pyongyang continues to reject disarmament ahead of possible nuclear talks with Washington. Speculation has grown over a possible meeting between US President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un during next month’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China, following repeated overtures by Trump for renewed nuclear negotiations. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun and Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi reaffirmed their position during a meeting on Friday on the sidelines of the Group of 20 (G20) gathering in Atlanta, Georgia. Advertisement According to the US State Department, the three officials “reaffirmed their resolute commitment to the complete denuclearization” of North Korea. They also pledged to ensure the “full implementation” of United Nations Security Council resolutions, including measures prohibiting support for revenue-generating activities linked to North Korea’s nuclear and ballistic missile programmes. Despite years of international sanctions, North Korea, which enjoys support from Russia and China, has legally entrenched its status as a nuclear-armed state. Its government has repeatedly insisted that its nuclear arsenal is permanent and irreversible. Advertisement Trump open to meeting Kim Trump has repeatedly expressed willingness to engage Pyongyang in nuclear negotiations while reducing joint military exercises with South Korea, a key US ally. The US president departed from longstanding American policy last year when he acknowledged that North Korea was already “sort of a nuclear power”. He also signalled that he was “100 percent” open to meeting Kim, although the North Korean leader did not respond to the proposal. Advertisement Analysts and South Korea’s intelligence agency believe Kim may have communicated Pyongyang’s position on possible talks with Trump to Beijing during a recent visit to the Chinese border city of Dandong. South Korea’s President Lee Jae Myung, who has adopted a more conciliatory approach towards Pyongyang, has repeatedly called for dialogue without preconditions. In September, Lee suggested that Washington consider pursuing a freeze on North Korea’s nuclear programme rather than demanding its immediate dismantlement, in exchange for sanctions relief. Advertisement However, critics argue that such a proposal could amount to tacit recognition of North Korea as a nuclear-armed state while allowing Pyongyang to secure sanctions relief without surrendering its weapons. Some analysts also believe China may be moving towards accepting North Korea’s nuclear status, citing the absence of references to denuclearisation in statements issued after Kim met Chinese President Xi Jinping in June. Meanwhile, Pyongyang on Saturday criticised a joint statement issued by a group of countries monitoring the implementation of sanctions against it. Advertisement North Korea insisted that “the stereotyped sanctions racket of the US and the West can neither influence the position of the DPRK (North Korea) as a nuclear weapons state”.
